content: In 1991, the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF introduced the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) to encourage maternity and newborn care facilities worldwide to adopt the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding. Facilities that fully adhered to these steps and complied with the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, as well as relevant World Health Assembly (WHA) resolutions, could earn the designation of Baby-Friendly. WHO published evidence supporting each of the Ten Steps in 1998, emphasizing the critical importance of the first hours and days of a newborn's life for establishing breastfeeding and providing mothers with the necessary support. Global health policy documents have consistently highlighted the significance of the Ten Steps. WHA resolutions in 1994 and 1996 called for specific actions related to the BFHI, and the 2002 Global Strategy for Infant and Young Child Feeding urged all maternity and newborn care facilities to implement the Ten Steps. In 2005, during the 15th anniversary of the Innocenti Declaration, a call to action was issued to revitalize the BFHI, expand its application to include neonatal and child health services, and provide community-based support for breastfeeding mothers and caregivers. The BFHI package was updated in 2006 and relaunched in 2009, incorporating new evidence for certain steps (e.g., Steps 4 and 8) and addressing the needs of women living with HIV. It also introduced guidelines for mother-friendly care and breastfeeding-friendly practices in other facilities and communities. Updated training and assessment tools were also provided. Research has demonstrated the significant impact of the BFHI on breastfeeding success. For example, a randomized trial in Belarus in the late 1990s showed that hospitals implementing the Ten Steps increased exclusive breastfeeding rates at three months to 43%, compared to 6% in non-intervention hospitals. A 2016 systematic review of 58 studies confirmed that adherence to the Ten Steps improves breastfeeding outcomes, including early initiation, exclusivity, and duration. Avoiding supplementation with non-breast milk (Step 6) and providing community support (Step 10) were identified as critical factors in sustaining breastfeeding rates. Despite its successes, the BFHI has faced challenges. By 2017, only about 10% of babies worldwide were born in facilities currently designated as Baby-Friendly, although many facilities implemented some of the Ten Steps without achieving full designation. National leadership, facility-level adaptation, and ongoing monitoring were identified as key factors for successful implementation. However, sustainability has been a challenge, with many facilities reverting to old practices over time due to a lack of regular monitoring systems. The revised BFHI guidance in 2018 aimed to address these challenges by simplifying the steps and making them more feasible for all facilities. For example, Step 2 now focuses on competency-based staff training rather than specific curricula, and Step 9 emphasizes counseling mothers on the use of feeding bottles and pacifiers rather than outright prohibition. The revised guidance also integrates the Ten Steps into broader maternal and newborn health programs, ensuring equitable access to high-quality care for all infants. The updated Ten Steps include critical management procedures, such as compliance with the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes, having a written infant feeding policy, and establishing ongoing monitoring systems. Key clinical practices include discussing breastfeeding with pregnant women, facilitating immediate skin-to-skin contact, supporting mothers in breastfeeding initiation and maintenance, avoiding unnecessary supplementation, enabling rooming-in, and coordinating post-discharge care. The BFHI has been transformative for many facilities, improving patient-centered care, staff attitudes, and breastfeeding support. However, challenges remain, including reliance on individual champions, insufficient pre-service training, and difficulties in sustaining changes. Full compliance with the International Code and fostering community breastfeeding support groups have also proven challenging. Moving forward, achieving widespread adherence to the Ten Steps will require renewed efforts, sustainable systems, and integration into national standards of care.
